activities.anchor: The classic way to see through the complexity
activities.caption: file each event by the flow it rides
activities.name: scFlowsBuckets

config.prompt: Three flows run through every chain — file each event:

items.label: ore becomes steel becomes parts becomes product becomes delivery
the customer's payment split into everyone's revenue on the way back
availability, lead times and shipment status travelling upstream-to-downstream
the returns that now define e-commerce
the empty toilet-paper shelves of 2020 — every link ordering extra against the same rumour

config.why: Nearly every famous supply chain failure is a flow problem, not a box problem — information late, distorted or absent.

activities.anchor: the semiconductor plant sees orders from assemblers
activities.caption: which curve matches the demand signal upstream?
activities.name: scSignalTrace

config.prompt: The true-demand signal as it moves upstream through the tiers — which profile matches?

curves.label: signal arrives intact at every tier
upstream sees final demand more clearly

config.why: Each layer in between injects its own noise — most companies cannot see final demand at all, and everything upstream is derived from it.

activities.anchor: Managed well, the chain is invisible
activities.caption: walk the trade-off triangle
activities.name: scTriangleBranch

config.root: Every decision from network design to purchase-order size lives inside the triangle: service level, inventory, cost.

start.text: Your chain promises near-perfect availability AND holds minimal inventory. Which corner collects the bill?

choices.label: Cost — pay for speed: air freight, duplicate suppliers, buffer capacity
None — a well-run chain gets all three

cost.text: You can perform brilliantly on any two; the third collects the bill — most supply chain arguments are really arguments about which corner to sacrifice.

choices.label: Now the mismatch case: an efficient chain serving fashion

free-lunch.text: The triangle forbids it — near-perfect availability with minimal inventory is only bought by paying for speed somewhere else.

mismatch.text: Chronic stockouts of the hits and mountains of the misses — Fisher's 1997 match says innovative products deserve responsive chains that buy speed even at higher cost.

config.why: The responsive chain serving detergent simply costs more than the competition can match — the mismatch fails in the other direction.

activities.anchor: Underneath the flows sits a strategic choice
activities.caption: pair each product with its chain
activities.name: scFisherMatch

config.prompt: Fisher's 1997 match — pair the product with the chain it deserves:

pairs.right: an efficient chain — squeeze cost, run full trucks, hold lean inventory
a responsive chain — buy speed and flexibility even at higher cost

pairs.left: the expensive failure for innovative products
pairs.right: the markdown bin full of last season's stock, not the air freight bill
chronic stockouts of the hits and mountains of the misses

config.why: Mismatched pairs are where supply chains visibly fail — match the chain to the product.

activities.anchor: a grocer turning stock 20 times a year
activities.caption: call the shelf-days behind the turns
activities.name: scTurnsEstimate

config.prompt: Inventory turns = cost of goods sold ÷ average inventory. A grocer turns stock 20 times a year. Roughly how many days of sales sit on its shelves?
config.why: 365 ÷ 20 ≈ 18 days — turns compress the whole inventory-versus-availability tension into one comparable figure; a heavy-equipment maker turning 2 times holds six months.
config.context: The other headline ratio, cash-to-cash, adds receivable days and subtracts payable days — it reveals whether growth consumes cash or releases it.

activities.anchor: which plots each purchased item by
activities.caption: walk the Kraljic quadrants
activities.name: scKraljicBranch

config.root: Four quadrants, four strategies — procurement effort is itself a scarce resource.

start.text: Item 1: the custom chips in a car maker's bill of materials — high profit impact, high supply risk. Your strategy?

choices.label: Partnership — joint development, long-term contracts, executive attention
choices.feedback: The quadrant treated as it deserves.

strategic-ok.text: Strategic quadrant, partnership — exactly the profile (high impact, high risk) that justifies the executive time.

choices.label: Item 2: commodity packaging — high impact, low risk

strategic-wrong.text: Catalogues for custom silicon — that is the non-critical treatment. The matrix files these chips as strategic (high impact, high risk): partnership, joint development, long-term contracts.

choices.label: Re-file, then item 2: commodity packaging — high impact, low risk

packaging.text: High impact, low risk — many suppliers could make it. Your strategy?

choices.label: Competition — market testing, aggressive negotiation, multiple bidders

leverage-ok.text: Leverage quadrant, competition — high impact means it is worth negotiating hard; low risk means you can walk away. The corporate world's cautionary tale is teams doing exactly this while strategic suppliers drift toward failure unwatched.

leverage-wrong.text: Buffer stock is bottleneck treatment — packaging is a leverage item (high impact, low risk): competition, multiple bidders, aggressive negotiation.

config.why: Price is one column of the matrix, not the whole of it — spend effort where the risk-and-value profile justifies it.

activities.anchor: every chain must choose where to hold its inventory
activities.caption: place the decoupling point for each chain
activities.name: scDecouplePlace

config.prompt: Where does final customer demand "enter" the process? Place a laptop chain (hold modules, configure at the last step):
config.why: Assemble-to-order: groceries push finished goods to a warehouse (make-to-stock), aircraft begin production on the order itself (make-to-order) — and the postponement principle says keep product generic as long as possible, which is why a global apparel brand ships undyed fabric and colours it after early sales data arrives.
